# Demographic Shifts & Socioeconomic Factors {#sec-demographics}

<!-- Purpose: demographic shifts and socioeconomic context for housing demand (PLAN.md §7 Ch 2).
     Narrative: prose migrated from the team's Google Doc draft (Oct 2026); numbers audited against the data. -->

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
library(tigris)

decennial <- read_rds("data/decennial.rds")
pep       <- read_rds("data/pep.rds")
demo      <- read_rds("data/acs_demographics.rds")
inc       <- read_rds("data/acs_income.rds")
fred      <- read_rds("data/fred.rds")
qcew      <- read_rds("data/qcew.rds")
lodes     <- read_rds("data/lodes.rds")
wf        <- read_rds("data/acs_workforce.rds")

# Palette anchors (match ggtext subtitle spans to fills)
blue   <- hda_pal[1]
green  <- hda_pal[2]
yellow <- hda_pal[3]
coral  <- hda_pal[4]

# Label the four benchmark + focus counties consistently
area_lab <- function(fips) case_when(
  fips == "51061" ~ "Fauquier",
  fips == "51047" ~ "Culpeper",
  fips == "51153" ~ "Prince William",
  fips == "51107" ~ "Loudoun",
  fips %in% c("51000", "51") ~ "Virginia"
)

# Shared age frame (F3) — expose a couple of scalars for bullet text
age <- demo$b01001 |> mutate(share = estimate / sum(estimate), .by = GEOID)
f_1834  <- age$share[age$GEOID == fauquier & age$age_band == "18-34"]
va_1834 <- age$share[age$GEOID == virginia & age$age_band == "18-34"]
f_65    <- sum(age$share[age$GEOID == fauquier & age$age_band %in% c("65-74", "75+")])
va_65   <- sum(age$share[age$GEOID == virginia & age$age_band %in% c("65-74", "75+")])

# PEP growth scalars (Vintage 2025)
pep_cty  <- pep$pop |> filter(variable == "POPESTIMATE")
pep_chg  <- pep$pop |> filter(variable == "NPOPCHG")
warr_pep <- pep$places |> filter(GEOID == towns[["warrenton"]])
cty_gain_20_25  <- diff(pep_cty$value[pep_cty$year %in% c(2020, max(pep_cty$year))])
warr_gain_20_25 <- diff(warr_pep$value[warr_pep$year %in% c(2020, max(warr_pep$year))])
chg_2021        <- pep_chg$value[pep_chg$year == 2021]
chg_recent      <- mean(pep_chg$value[pep_chg$year >= 2022])
warr_latest     <- warr_pep$value[warr_pep$year == max(warr_pep$year)]
```

## Population growth

Fauquier has seen steady population growth over the last 35 years, despite consistent descriptions of the county's similarities over time. Those that grew up in Fauquier still recognize it as the place where they were raised. Fauquier's population climbed from 48,741 in 1990 to about 76,500 in 2025, a 57% increase, adding some 27,800 residents over 35 years.

Growth throughout has been steady rather than explosive: after a 2021 jump of about `r label_comma()(round(chg_2021, -1))` residents, the county has added about `r label_comma()(round(chg_recent, -2))` a year since 2022. Warrenton has held at about `r label_comma()(round(warr_latest, -2))` people since 2022, and Bealeton reached nearly 5,000 by 2024. Both towns together hold about a fifth of the county's residents, but nearly all recent growth has occurred outside them: of the county's `r label_comma()(cty_gain_20_25)` added residents from 2020 to 2025, Warrenton accounts for just `r label_comma()(warr_gain_20_25)`.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Caveat: mixed sources and universes
The county line splices decennial 100% counts (April 1: 1990, 2000, 2010, 2020) with Population Estimates Program figures (July 1: 2021–2025); Warrenton's recent points are also PEP, while Bealeton's 2024 point is an ACS 5-year estimate. These are different universes and reference dates — small level differences between series are expected, not real change. Bealeton has no 2000 decennial place record and is not published in the PEP, so its line starts in 2010; its apparent dip from the 2020 count to the 2024 ACS estimate likely reflects that change of source rather than population loss. Documented in @sec-data-notes.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-population
#| fig-cap: "Fauquier has grown steadily for three decades"
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of Fauquier County's population from 1990 to 2025, rising from about 48,700 to 76,500 across decennial counts and annual estimates. Two lower lines track the towns from 2010: Warrenton rises from about 9,600 to 10,200 and has been flat since 2022, while Bealeton goes from about 4,400 to 5,900 in 2020 and about 5,000 in the 2024 ACS estimate."

county_line <- bind_rows(
  decennial$pop |> filter(GEOID == fauquier) |>
    transmute(year, pop = value, src = "Decennial count"),
  pep$pop |> filter(GEOID == fauquier, variable == "POPESTIMATE", year > 2020) |>
    transmute(year, pop = value, src = "Estimate")
) |> arrange(year)

towns_line <- bind_rows(
  decennial$pop |> filter(geo_type == "place", year %in% c(2010, 2020)) |>
    transmute(GEOID, year, pop = value, src = "Decennial count"),
  demo$b01003 |> filter(geo_type == "place", GEOID == towns[["bealeton"]]) |>
    transmute(GEOID, year = 2024L, pop = estimate, src = "Estimate"),
  pep$places |> filter(year > 2020) |>
    transmute(GEOID, year, pop = value, src = "Estimate")
) |> mutate(geo = if_else(GEOID == "5183136", "Warrenton", "Bealeton")) |> arrange(year)

ggplot(mapping = aes(year, pop)) +
  geom_line(data = county_line, color = blue, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = county_line, aes(shape = src), color = blue, size = 2.4) +
  geom_line(data = towns_line, aes(group = geo), color = coral, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(data = towns_line, aes(shape = src), color = coral, size = 2) +
  geom_text(data = filter(county_line, year == max(year)),
            aes(label = "Fauquier County"), color = blue, fontface = "bold",
            hjust = 1, vjust = -1.3, size = 3.4) +
  geom_text(data = slice_max(towns_line, year, by = geo), aes(label = geo),
            color = coral, hjust = -0.15, size = 3, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Decennial count" = 16, "Estimate" = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma(), limits = c(0, 88000),
                     expand = expansion(c(0, 0.05))) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(1990, 2028), breaks = c(seq(1990, 2020, 10), 2025)) +
  labs(
    title = "Fauquier has grown steadily for three decades",
    subtitle = "Total population: decennial counts are solid points and estimates are open points",
    caption = paste0(
      "**Sources:** U.S. Census Bureau, Decennial Census, 1990–2020. ",
      "Population Estimates Program, Vintage 2025. 2020–2024 American Community Survey 5-year estimates.",
      "<br>**Note:** Bealeton 2024 is an ACS 5-year estimate (Table B01003)."
    ),
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda() +
  add_zero_line("y") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

With roughly `r label_comma()(round(chg_recent, -2))` or more residents gained yearly since 2021 and limited residential development areas, the sensation of housing scarcity is felt by newer and long-term residents alike.

## Components of change

```{r}
# Latest-year components (pep$components is a 2020–2025 series)
comp_25 <- pep$components |> filter(year == max(year))
cv <- \(v) comp_25$value[comp_25$variable == v]
nat_prev <- pep$components$value[pep$components$variable == "NATURALCHG" &
                                   pep$components$year == max(pep$components$year) - 1]
```

Net migration, people moving in from elsewhere, far outweighs natural change, births within the county compared with deaths, as the county's growth engine. The county grows chiefly because more people move in (+`r cv("NETMIG")`) than are born there (+`r cv("NATURALCHG")`). Natural increase is thin and shrinking: `r cv("BIRTHS")` births barely exceeded `r cv("DEATHS")` deaths, down from a natural gain of `r nat_prev` the year before, which is consistent with an aging population.

```{r}
#| label: fig-components
#| fig-cap: "Migration drives Fauquier's growth more than natural increase"
#| fig-alt: "Diverging horizontal bar chart of Fauquier County's components of population change for the year ending July 2025. Births add about 722 and deaths subtract about 665, for a small natural gain of 57; domestic migration adds 539 and international migration 47, for net migration of 586, the larger driver."

comp <- comp_25 |>
  filter(variable %in% c("BIRTHS", "DEATHS", "DOMESTICMIG", "INTERNATIONALMIG")) |>
  mutate(
    value = if_else(variable == "DEATHS", -value, value),
    label = case_when(
      variable == "BIRTHS"           ~ "Births",
      variable == "DEATHS"           ~ "Deaths",
      variable == "DOMESTICMIG"      ~ "Domestic migration",
      variable == "INTERNATIONALMIG" ~ "International migration"
    ),
    sign = if_else(value >= 0, "Adds population", "Reduces population")
  ) |>
  mutate(label = fct_reorder(label, value))

ggplot(comp, aes(value, label, fill = sign)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.68) +
  geom_text(aes(label = number(value, accuracy = 1, style_positive = "plus")),
            hjust = ifelse(comp$value >= 0, -0.15, 1.15), size = 3.2, color = "grey20") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Adds population" = green, "Reduces population" = coral)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma(), limits = c(-750, 900), expand = expansion(c(0.08, 0.12))) +
  labs(
    title = "Migration drives Fauquier's growth more than natural increase",
    subtitle = paste0("Net migration of +", cv("NETMIG"), " vs natural change of +", cv("NATURALCHG"),
                      ", one year ending July 1, 2025"),
    caption = pep_cap(2025), x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda(flip_gridlines = TRUE) +
  add_zero_line("x") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Migration is overwhelmingly domestic (+`r cv("DOMESTICMIG")`) with a smaller international component (+`r cv("INTERNATIONALMIG")`). People relocate to Fauquier from elsewhere in the U.S., largely the D.C. metro.

## Age structure

As implied by natural population change, Fauquier has a notably thin young-adult band: just `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(f_1834)` of residents are 18–34, versus `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(va_1834)` statewide. Young adults tend to leave and often do not return, a pattern tied to a lack of viable positions and entry-level housing (see @sec-market-ownership and @fig-employment).

The county skews toward established working-age adults: 35–64-year-olds are its largest group, feeding demand for family-sized housing. Seniors are a modestly larger and growing share of Fauquier's population: `r label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)(f_65)` are 65+, edging above Virginia's `r label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)(va_65)` and rising, as the 35–64 cohort ages in place.

```{r}
#| label: fig-age
#| fig-cap: "Fauquier has fewer young adults than Virginia"
#| fig-alt: "Grouped bar chart comparing the age distribution of Fauquier County and Virginia. Fauquier has a smaller share of adults 18 to 34 (13% versus 16% statewide) and slightly larger shares of children and of adults 35 to 64. Shares of residents 65 to 74 and 75 and older are nearly identical."

age_lvls <- c("Under 18", "18–34", "35–64", "65–74", "75+")
age_cv <- age |>
  filter(geo_type %in% c("county", "state")) |>
  mutate(geo = if_else(GEOID == fauquier, "Fauquier County", "Virginia"),
         age_band = factor(str_replace(age_band, "-", "–"), levels = age_lvls))

ggplot(age_cv, aes(age_band, share, fill = geo)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label_percent(accuracy = 1)(share)),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.72), vjust = -0.4, size = 2.9, color = "grey25") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1), expand = expansion(c(0, 0.08))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Fauquier County" = blue, "Virginia" = "grey70")) +
  labs(
    title = "Fauquier has fewer young adults than Virginia",
    subtitle = "Share of population by age group, <span style='color:#445ca9'>**Fauquier County**</span> vs <span style='color:#b3b3b3'>**Virginia**</span>, 2024",
    caption = acs_cap("B01001"), x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda() +
  add_zero_line("y") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {.callout-note title="What we heard"}
Interviewees said young people who leave Fauquier typically do not return, for lack of viable jobs and entry-level housing. They wondered how to recruit young people to the county while also helping seniors age in place.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Town spotlight — two very different age profiles
The towns diverge in age sharply. **Warrenton is the county's oldest community**: about 18% are 65 and older (High reliability). **Bealeton is markedly younger**, with roughly 7–8% seniors and a large under-18 share, reflecting its role as a family-oriented growth node.
:::

## Households

Married-couple families represent 60% of Fauquier's households, well above Virginia's 49%, with an average household size of 2.78, also larger than the state's 2.52.

```{r}
#| label: fig-households
#| fig-cap: "Warrenton has far more people living alone than the county"
#| fig-alt: "Stacked bar chart of household composition for Fauquier County, its two towns, and Virginia. Married-couple families are the largest share in Fauquier, Bealeton, and Virginia, while in Warrenton people living alone are the single largest group at about 41%, nearly double the county share of 22%."

hh_lab <- c(B11001_003 = "Married-couple family", B11001_004 = "Other family",
            B11001_008 = "Living alone",          B11001_009 = "Other non-family")
hh <- demo$b11001 |>
  filter(variable %in% names(hh_lab)) |>
  mutate(share = estimate / sum(estimate), .by = GEOID) |>
  mutate(
    type = factor(hh_lab[variable], levels = rev(unname(hh_lab))),
    geo = factor(case_when(
      GEOID == fauquier   ~ "Fauquier County",
      GEOID == "5183136"  ~ "Warrenton",
      GEOID == "5105336"  ~ "Bealeton",
      GEOID == virginia   ~ "Virginia"
    ), levels = c("Virginia", "Bealeton", "Warrenton", "Fauquier County"))
  )

size_lab <- demo$b25010 |>
  filter(variable == "B25010_001") |>
  transmute(geo = case_when(GEOID == fauquier ~ "Fauquier County", GEOID == "5183136" ~ "Warrenton",
                            GEOID == "5105336" ~ "Bealeton", GEOID == virginia ~ "Virginia"),
            avg = estimate)

hh_fill <- c("Married-couple family" = blue, "Other family" = green,
             "Living alone" = coral, "Other non-family" = "grey75")

ggplot(hh, aes(share, geo, fill = type)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(data = size_lab, aes(x = 1.02, y = geo, label = paste0(number(avg, accuracy = 0.01), " people")),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = 0, size = 2.9, color = "grey35") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_percent(), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25),
                     expand = expansion(c(0, 0.2))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = hh_fill) +
  labs(
    title = "Warrenton has far more people living alone than the county",
    subtitle = "Household composition by type, with average household size, 2024",
    caption = paste0("**Source:** U.S. Census Bureau, 2020–2024 American Community Survey ",
                     "5-year estimates, Tables B11001 and B25010."),
    x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda(flip_gridlines = TRUE) +
  theme(legend.position = "top") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 1, reverse = TRUE))
```

Warrenton looks structurally different: people living alone are its single largest household type (41%), and its average household is just 2.49. This profiles Warrenton as a center for small-town rentals that can serve aging seniors.

Bealeton runs the other way: family-heavy (54% married-couple) with the largest average household (3.11), pointing to demand for larger, family-sized homes.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Reliability
Town composition shares are Medium reliability (CV 15–30%) for most categories — Bealeton's "other non-family" slice is Low (CV > 30%) — so read the town bars as broad profiles, not precise shares. Both towns' average household sizes are High reliability.
:::

## Household income

At $130,189 annually, Fauquier's median household income is the third-highest of its peer set, after Prince William and Loudoun. Fauquier is essentially tied with Prince William in median income and is far below fast-growing Loudoun ($181,765).

```{r}
#| label: fig-income-levels
#| fig-cap: "Fauquier's median income ranks third among its peers"
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart of 2024 median household income. Loudoun leads at about $182,000, followed by Prince William at $131,000 and Fauquier at $130,000, then Bealeton ($108,000), Culpeper ($100,000), Virginia ($93,000), and Warrenton ($83,000)."

lvls <- inc$b19013_trend |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  mutate(place = str_remove(NAME, " (County|town|CDP),.*$") |> str_replace("Virginia", "Virginia"),
         place = case_when(GEOID == fauquier ~ "Fauquier", GEOID == "51153" ~ "Prince William",
                           GEOID == "51107" ~ "Loudoun", GEOID == "51047" ~ "Culpeper",
                           GEOID == "5183136" ~ "Warrenton", GEOID == "5105336" ~ "Bealeton",
                           GEOID == virginia ~ "Virginia"),
         grp = case_when(GEOID == fauquier ~ "Fauquier",
                         GEOID %in% unname(towns) ~ "Town", .default = "Other")) |>
  mutate(place = fct_reorder(place, estimate))

ggplot(lvls, aes(estimate, place, fill = grp)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label_dollar(accuracy = 1000)(estimate)),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3, color = "grey25") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k"),
                     expand = expansion(c(0, 0.18))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Fauquier = blue, Town = coral, Other = "grey75"), guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Fauquier's median income ranks third among its peers",
    subtitle = "Median household income, 2024: <span style='color:#445ca9'>**Fauquier**</span> and <span style='color:#e76f52'>**study towns**</span> vs benchmarks",
    caption = acs_cap("B19013"), x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda(flip_gridlines = TRUE)
```

Conversely, Warrenton's median income, $83,331, is the lowest in the comparison and below the statewide median income of $93,170. Bealeton's median income of $108,224 lands between the two. High county-wide income coexists with a lower-income Warrenton core, while Bealeton tracks closer to the county: a spatial income gap that shapes where affordability pressure concentrates.

::: {.callout-note title="What we heard"}
Interviewees described the county's wealth as held in its rural areas and concentrated in the northernmost part of the county, closest to the highways that connect commuters to higher wages in D.C.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Reliability
Warrenton's median is High reliability (CV 5%); Bealeton's is Medium (CV 17%, ±$30,504), so its position relative to the county should be read as approximate.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-income-real
#| fig-cap: "Real incomes have risen only modestly after adjusting for inflation"
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of Fauquier County median household income from 2010 to 2024. The nominal line rises steeply from about $84,000 to $130,000, while the inflation-adjusted line in 2024 dollars rises much more gently from about $114,000 to $130,000."

cpi24 <- fred$cpi$cpi_less_shelter[fred$cpi$year == 2024]
real <- inc$b19013_trend |>
  filter(GEOID == fauquier) |>
  left_join(fred$cpi, by = "year") |>
  transmute(year,
            Nominal = estimate,
            `Real (2024 $)` = estimate * cpi24 / cpi_less_shelter) |>
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "series", values_to = "income")

ggplot(real, aes(year, income, color = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Nominal" = "grey55", "Real (2024 $)" = blue)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k"), limits = c(0, 140000), breaks = seq(0, 140000, 20000),
                     expand = expansion(c(0, 0.05))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2010, 2024, 2)) +
  labs(
    title = "Real incomes have risen only modestly after adjusting for inflation",
    subtitle = "Fauquier median household income, <span style='color:#8c8c8c'>**nominal**</span> vs <span style='color:#445ca9'>**inflation-adjusted (2024 $)**</span>, 2010–2024",
    caption = paste0(acs_cap("B19013", "2006–2010 through 2020–2024"), "<br>**Note:** ", cpi_cap()), x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda() +
  add_zero_line("y") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Nominal median income rose 55% over 2010–2024 from $83,877 → $130,189, but most of that reflects inflation. In constant 2024 dollars, real income only grew about 15% with real buying power creeping up, not surging, even as home prices climbed far faster (see @sec-market-ownership).

Fauquier as a whole is high-income: 44% of households earn $150,000 or more — nearly double Virginia's share of high earners. Warrenton is the lower-income town: about 27% of its households earn under $50,000 per year versus 17% of households county-wide. Warrenton also has the smallest share of earners in the top ($150k+) bracket.

```{r}
#| label: fig-income-dist
#| fig-cap: "Warrenton households skew lower-income than Bealeton or the county"
#| fig-alt: "Grouped bar chart of household income distribution across six brackets for Fauquier County, Warrenton, Bealeton, and Virginia. Warrenton has the largest share of households under $50,000, while Fauquier and Bealeton concentrate in the $150,000-and-up bracket. Bealeton's lowest three brackets are suppressed for low reliability."

band_lvls <- c("< $25k", "$25–50k", "$50–75k", "$75–100k", "$100–150k", "$150k+")
geo_lvls  <- c("Fauquier County", "Warrenton", "Bealeton", "Virginia")
dist <- inc$b19001 |>
  mutate(share = estimate / sum(estimate), .by = GEOID) |>
  flag_reliability() |>
  mutate(
    geo = factor(case_when(GEOID == fauquier ~ "Fauquier County", GEOID == "5183136" ~ "Warrenton",
                           GEOID == "5105336" ~ "Bealeton", GEOID == virginia ~ "Virginia"),
                 levels = geo_lvls),
    inc_band = factor(str_replace(inc_band, "-", "–"), levels = band_lvls),
    # Bealeton floor: suppress Low-reliability (CV > 30%) cells
    share = if_else(reliability == "Low", NA_real_, share)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(geo))

ggplot(dist, aes(inc_band, share, fill = geo)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.78) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1), expand = expansion(c(0, 0.06))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Fauquier County" = blue, "Warrenton" = coral,
                               "Bealeton" = yellow, "Virginia" = "grey70")) +
  labs(
    title = "Warrenton households skew lower-income than Bealeton or the county",
    subtitle = paste0("Share of households by income bracket, 2024:<br>",
                      "<span style='color:#445ca9'>**Fauquier County**</span>, ",
                      "<span style='color:#e76f52'>**Warrenton**</span>, ",
                      "<span style='color:#e9ab3f'>**Bealeton**</span>, and ",
                      "<span style='color:#b3b3b3'>**Virginia**</span>"),
    caption = paste0(acs_cap("B19001"),
                     "<br>**Note:** Bealeton's three lowest brackets are suppressed (CV above 30%) and appear as gaps."),
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda() +
  add_zero_line("y") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Bealeton mirrors the county more closely, concentrated in the upper-middle and $150k+ income brackets, consistent with its higher median income.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Reliability
Bealeton's three lowest income brackets carry coefficients of variation above 30% and are suppressed here; the shown Warrenton and Bealeton cells are Medium-to-High reliability.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Poverty — county low, town contrast
Fauquier's overall **poverty rate** is 6.8% (about 5,000 people), which is below Virginia's 9.9%. The town rates are less certain and are best read as counts: roughly 950 people live in poverty in Warrenton and 80 in Bealeton, with margins too wide to publish reliable place-level rates (both CV > 30%). The takeaway is directional — poverty is low county-wide and modestly concentrated in Warrenton.[^acs-poverty]
:::

[^acs-poverty]: Source: ACS 2020–2024, Table S1701 (S1701_C01_001 universe, S1701_C02_001 count, S1701_C03_001 rate).

## Employment

```{r}
# QCEW 2025 annual scalars for prose
fq_tot  <- qcew$total |> filter(area_fips == fauquier, own_code == "0")
jobs_15 <- fq_tot$annual_avg_emplvl[fq_tot$year == 2015]
jobs_25 <- fq_tot$annual_avg_emplvl[fq_tot$year == 2025]
pay_all <- \(fips) qcew$total$avg_annual_pay[qcew$total$area_fips == fips & qcew$total$own_code == "0" &
                                               qcew$total$year == 2025]
fq_sector_pay <- \(naics) qcew$sector |>
  filter(area_fips == fauquier, own_code == "5", industry_code == naics, year == 2025) |> pull(avg_annual_pay)
k <- \(x) label_dollar()(round(x, -2))   # e.g. $60,100
```

The county is a modest job center relative to its neighbors to the north and east: it adds workers steadily, but has not captured the metro's fastest employment expansion. That said, Fauquier's at-place employment grew from `r label_comma()(jobs_15)` jobs in 2015 to `r label_comma()(jobs_25)` in 2025, an increase of about `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(jobs_25 / jobs_15 - 1)`.

This growth roughly matches the statewide pace, but is well behind Loudoun, which saw about a 33% increase in employment, alongside a 19% increase in employment for Prince William for the same time period.

```{r}
#| label: fig-employment
#| fig-cap: "Fauquier's job base has grown but slower than its metro neighbors"
#| fig-alt: "Indexed line chart of at-place employment from 2015 to 2025, set to 100 in 2015. Loudoun rises fastest to about 133, Prince William to 119, while Fauquier and Virginia track together near 111 and Culpeper trails at about 105."

emp <- qcew$total |>
  filter(own_code == "0") |>
  mutate(area = area_lab(area_fips)) |>
  mutate(idx = annual_avg_emplvl / annual_avg_emplvl[year == 2015] * 100, .by = area_fips)

# End labels: Fauquier and Virginia finish within 0.1 of each other, so nudge them apart
emp_lab <- emp |> filter(year == 2025) |>
  mutate(idx_lab = idx + case_when(area == "Fauquier" ~ -1.3, area == "Virginia" ~ 1.3, .default = 0))

ggplot(emp, aes(year, idx, color = area)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_line(aes(linewidth = area == "Fauquier")) +
  geom_text(data = emp_lab, aes(y = idx_lab, label = area), hjust = -0.05, size = 3, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Fauquier" = blue, "Culpeper" = "grey70", "Prince William" = "grey70",
                                "Loudoun" = "grey70", "Virginia" = "grey45")) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 1.3, `FALSE` = 0.7), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2015, 2025, 2), limits = c(2015, 2028)) +
  labs(
    title = "Fauquier's job base has grown but slower than its metro neighbors",
    subtitle = "At-place employment indexed to 2015 = 100 for Fauquier and comparison areas",
    caption = qcew_cap("2015–2025"), x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Slower job growth reinforces the commute-out pattern — many residents work in higher-growth counties to the east (see @fig-commute-out).

Fauquier's all-jobs average pay was about `r label_dollar()(round(pay_all(fauquier), -3))` in 2025, which is mid-pack among its peers, with Culpeper at `r k(pay_all(benchmarks[["culpeper"]]))` and Prince William near `r label_dollar()(round(pay_all(benchmarks[["prince_william"]]), -3))`, but far below Loudoun with `r k(pay_all(benchmarks[["loudoun"]]))`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-wages
#| fig-cap: "Only Loudoun outpays Fauquier across all jobs"
#| fig-alt: "Grouped bar chart of 2025 average annual pay by industry for Fauquier and three benchmark counties. Loudoun pays the most in every industry shown, at about $87,000 across all jobs against $68,000 in Fauquier. Fauquier ranks second on all jobs, health care, and retail, and third on local government. Retail trade is the lowest-paying sector in every county."

ind_lvls <- c("All jobs", "Health care", "Local government", "Retail trade")
wages <- bind_rows(
  qcew$total     |> filter(own_code == "0", agglvl_code == "70", year == 2025) |>
    transmute(area_fips, industry = "All jobs", pay = avg_annual_pay),
  qcew$sector    |> filter(own_code == "5", agglvl_code == "74", industry_code == "62", year == 2025) |>
    transmute(area_fips, industry = "Health care", pay = avg_annual_pay),
  qcew$ownership |> filter(own_code == "3", agglvl_code == "71", year == 2025) |>
    transmute(area_fips, industry = "Local government", pay = avg_annual_pay),
  qcew$sector    |> filter(own_code == "5", agglvl_code == "74", industry_code == "44-45", year == 2025) |>
    transmute(area_fips, industry = "Retail trade", pay = avg_annual_pay)
) |>
  filter(area_fips %in% c(fauquier, unname(benchmarks))) |>
  mutate(area = factor(area_lab(area_fips), levels = c("Fauquier", "Culpeper", "Prince William", "Loudoun")),
         industry = factor(industry, levels = ind_lvls))

ggplot(wages, aes(industry, pay, fill = area)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.78) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k"), limits = c(0, 100000),
                     expand = expansion(c(0, 0.05))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Fauquier" = blue, "Culpeper" = "grey85",
                               "Prince William" = "grey70", "Loudoun" = "grey50")) +
  labs(
    title = "Only Loudoun outpays Fauquier across all jobs",
    subtitle = "Average annual pay by industry, 2025: <span style='color:#445ca9'>**Fauquier**</span> vs benchmark counties",
    caption = qcew_cap("2025"), x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda() +
  add_zero_line("y") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The county's largest employers by sector are local government (including the school systems), retail, health care, and construction. Most pay modestly: health care averaged `r k(fq_sector_pay("62"))` yearly and retail trade just `r k(fq_sector_pay("44-45"))`, the lowest-paying of the sectors shown in every county; only accommodation and food service pays less locally, at about `r k(fq_sector_pay("72"))`. Construction is the exception at about `r k(fq_sector_pay("23"))`. Wage growth has kept pace with neighbors, with all four counties seeing all-jobs pay rise 42–48% since 2015 (QCEW trend 2015→2025, not shown in the chart above).

Wage growth has held along neighboring counties. The gap is one of level, not trajectory — Fauquier simply has fewer of the high-wage jobs concentrated to its east and little diversity in its employment sectors.

::: {.callout-note title="What we heard"}
Interviewees saw worker opportunity, housing, and economic development as tightly linked. They described an in-county job base that is mostly low-wage, where higher-paying employers have been pushed out by a self-reinforcing cycle: without middle-income jobs, middle-income housing demand stays suppressed, and without that housing, employers struggle to recruit workers who can afford what is available. As one put it, "Fauquier is a bedroom community - people live here and work elsewhere."
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## A note on the wage figures
FHFH-computed 2025 QCEW averages run modestly above the Greater Piedmont REALTOR's study's earlier $64,272 all-jobs figure (2023 vintage) — the difference is nominal wage growth between vintages, not a discrepancy. Small county-by-sector cells that BLS suppresses for disclosure are excluded, so only complete series (all jobs, health care, local government, retail trade) are shown.
:::

### Early 2026: jobs edge up, wages jump

```{r}
# Same-quarter comparison (2025 Q1 vs 2026 Q1); never mixed with the annual series above.
# Annual wage = average weekly wage x 52.
q <- qcew$quarterly |>
  mutate(vintage = if_else(year == max(year), "new", "old"))
stopifnot(length(unique(q$qtr)) == 1, n_distinct(q$year) == 2)
q_new <- paste(max(q$year),     paste0("Q", unique(q$qtr)))
q_old <- paste(max(q$year) - 1, paste0("Q", unique(q$qtr)))

q_area <- q |>
  filter(own_code == "0", agglvl_code %in% c("50", "70")) |>
  select(area_fips, vintage, avg_emplvl, avg_wkly_wage) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = vintage, values_from = c(avg_emplvl, avg_wkly_wage)) |>
  transmute(
    area      = factor(area_lab(area_fips),
                       levels = c("Fauquier", "Culpeper", "Prince William", "Loudoun", "Virginia")),
    jobs      = avg_emplvl_new,
    jobs_chg  = avg_emplvl_new - avg_emplvl_old,
    jobs_pct  = avg_emplvl_new / avg_emplvl_old - 1,
    wage      = avg_wkly_wage_new * 52,
    wage_pct  = avg_wkly_wage_new / avg_wkly_wage_old - 1
  ) |>
  arrange(area)

sector_names <- c(
  "11" = "Agriculture", "22" = "Utilities", "23" = "Construction", "31-33" = "Manufacturing",
  "42" = "Wholesale trade", "44-45" = "Retail trade", "48-49" = "Transportation and warehousing",
  "51" = "Information", "52" = "Finance and insurance", "53" = "Real estate",
  "54" = "Professional and technical services", "56" = "Administrative services",
  "61" = "Educational services", "62" = "Health care", "71" = "Arts and recreation",
  "72" = "Accommodation and food services", "81" = "Other services"
)

q_sector <- q |>
  filter(area_fips == fauquier, own_code == "5", agglvl_code %in% c("54", "74"),
         is.na(disclosure_code) | disclosure_code != "N") |>
  select(industry_code, vintage, avg_emplvl, avg_wkly_wage) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = vintage, values_from = c(avg_emplvl, avg_wkly_wage)) |>
  filter(!is.na(avg_emplvl_new), !is.na(avg_emplvl_old)) |>
  transmute(
    sector   = coalesce(unname(sector_names[industry_code]), industry_code),
    code     = industry_code,
    jobs     = avg_emplvl_new,
    jobs_chg = avg_emplvl_new - avg_emplvl_old,
    jobs_pct = avg_emplvl_new / avg_emplvl_old - 1,
    wage     = avg_wkly_wage_new * 52,
    wage_pct = avg_wkly_wage_new / avg_wkly_wage_old - 1
  )

fq  <- q_area |> filter(area == "Fauquier")
cn  <- q_sector |> filter(code == "23")
hc  <- q_sector |> filter(code == "62")
pct <- label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)
pct0 <- label_percent(accuracy = 1)
```

Fauquier added about `r label_comma(accuracy = 10)(fq$jobs_chg)` jobs between `r q_old` and `r q_new`, up `r pct(fq$jobs_pct)` to roughly `r label_comma(accuracy = 100)(fq$jobs)`. That outpaces Culpeper and Virginia, where employment was flat, but trails Prince William and Loudoun. The number of private and public establishments did not change.

Average annual wages in Fauquier rose `r pct(fq$wage_pct)` over the same period, to `r label_dollar()(fq$wage)`, the fastest increase of any comparison area. Part of this reflects a few sectors. Construction wages rose `r pct0(cn$wage_pct)` as the sector added `r label_comma()(round(cn$jobs_chg))` jobs (`r pct0(cn$jobs_pct)`), the largest gain in the county and consistent with the rise in 2026 building permits (@sec-inventory). Health care went the other way, shedding about `r label_comma(accuracy = 10)(abs(hc$jobs_chg))` jobs (`r pct0(hc$jobs_pct)`), the largest loss.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q-area
#| tbl-cap: "Fauquier's jobs edged up while its wages rose faster than any neighbor's"
#| tbl-alt: "Table comparing jobs and annualized average wages in 2026 Q1 with 2025 Q1 for Fauquier, Culpeper, Prince William, Loudoun, and Virginia. Fauquier jobs rose 0.7 percent and wages 8.5 percent, the largest wage increase of the five areas."

chg_cell <- \(x, txt) cell_spec(txt, color = if_else(x >= 0, blue, coral), escape = FALSE)

q_area |>
  transmute(
    Area = as.character(area),
    jobs = label_comma()(round(jobs)),
    jobs_pct = chg_cell(jobs_pct, label_percent(accuracy = 0.1, style_positive = "plus", style_negative = "minus")(jobs_pct)),
    wage = label_dollar()(round(wage)),
    wage_pct = chg_cell(wage_pct, label_percent(accuracy = 0.1, style_positive = "plus", style_negative = "minus")(wage_pct))
  ) |>
  kbl(col.names = c("Area", q_new, paste("Change vs.", q_old), q_new, paste("Change vs.", q_old)),
      align = "lrrrr", escape = FALSE) |>
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Jobs" = 2, "Annual wage" = 2)) |>
  kable_styling(c("condensed", "striped"), full_width = FALSE) |>
  row_spec(1, bold = TRUE) |>
  footnote(
    general = tbl_note(paste0(
      qcew_cap(paste(q_old, "and", q_new), annual = FALSE),
      "<br>**Notes:** Annual wage is the average weekly wage times 52. Figures are for a single quarter, ",
      "are preliminary, and are not comparable to the annual pay averages above."
    )),
    general_title = "", footnote_as_chunk = TRUE, escape = FALSE
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q-sector
#| tbl-cap: "Construction added jobs in Fauquier while health care lost them"
#| tbl-alt: "Table of the five private-sector industries in Fauquier with the largest job changes between 2025 Q1 and 2026 Q1. Construction gained about 330 jobs; health care lost about 170, followed by retail trade, accommodation and food services, with a small gain in finance and insurance."

q_sector |>
  slice_max(abs(jobs_chg), n = 5) |>
  arrange(desc(jobs_chg)) |>
  transmute(
    Sector = sector,
    jobs = label_comma()(round(jobs)),
    jobs_chg = chg_cell(jobs_chg, number(jobs_chg, accuracy = 1, style_positive = "plus", style_negative = "minus")),
    wage = label_dollar()(round(wage))
  ) |>
  kbl(col.names = c("Sector", q_new, paste("Change vs.", q_old), q_new),
      align = "lrrr", escape = FALSE) |>
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Jobs" = 2, "Annual wage" = 1)) |>
  kable_styling(c("condensed", "striped"), full_width = FALSE) |>
  footnote(
    general = tbl_note(paste0(
      qcew_cap(paste(q_old, "and", q_new), annual = FALSE),
      "<br>**Notes:** Private ownership only. Sectors with suppressed cells are omitted. ",
      "Annual wage is the average weekly wage times 52."
    )),
    general_title = "", footnote_as_chunk = TRUE, escape = FALSE
  )
```

## Commuting

It's widely recognized that those who live in Fauquier do not work in Fauquier, impacting the local economy and housing opportunities in both directions. Fully 76.4% of Fauquier's employed residents commute out of the county: just 8,266 of the county's 35,028 employed residents work in Fauquier itself. Separately, only 35.4% of jobs located in Fauquier are filled by county residents (8,266 of 23,349 Fauquier jobs), two measures of the same bedroom-community pattern. The largest outbound flows run east into the D.C. job market: nearly 8,200 to Fairfax, 5,400 to Prince William, and 3,000 to Loudoun.

```{r}
#| label: fig-commute-out
#| fig-cap: "Fairfax and Prince William draw the most Fauquier out-commuters"
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart of the top counties where Fauquier residents work outside the county. Fairfax leads with about 8,200 workers, followed by Prince William at 5,400 and Loudoun at 3,000, then smaller flows of about 600 to 1,200 workers each to Manassas, Arlington, Culpeper, Stafford, and Alexandria."

xwalk <- fips_codes |>
  transmute(fips = paste0(state_code, county_code),
            county = str_remove(county, " County"))

out <- lodes$top_destinations |>
  transmute(fips = w_geocode, workers = S000) |>
  left_join(xwalk, by = "fips") |>
  slice_max(workers, n = 8) |>
  mutate(county = fct_reorder(county, workers))

ggplot(out, aes(workers, county)) +
  geom_col(fill = blue, width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label_comma()(workers)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3, color = "grey25") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma(), expand = expansion(c(0, 0.14))) +
  labs(
    title = "Fairfax and Prince William draw the most Fauquier out-commuters",
    subtitle = "Top destinations for employed Fauquier residents working outside the county, 2023",
    caption = lodes_cap(2023), x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda(flip_gridlines = TRUE)
```

Inbound commuting is the mirror image, but comparatively smaller for Fauquier. The top in-commuter origins are from Culpeper with 2,400 workers incoming daily, followed by Prince William with 2,300, and Fairfax at 1,300, filling local jobs Fauquier residents don't. The local government officials, teachers, nurses, and gas station attendants are typically driving in.

::: {.callout-note title="What we heard"}
Interviewees reiterated that this workforce gap is visible across sectors. More than half of Fauquier Health employees live outside the county, and teachers, firefighters, and government workers face the same commute. Wages suited to the local job base cannot carry local rents or mortgages, and housing suited to local workers is largely nonexistent.
:::

A large share of Fauquier's working residents, 37%, commute 45 minutes or more daily. This is more than double Virginia's rate of those who commute that long - 18%. This is a direct consequence of the out-commuting pattern outlined in @fig-commute-out.

Long commutes are a regional exurban trait: Culpeper has about 37% of its commuters traveling 45 minutes or more. Prince William looks similar at 36%, while inner-suburb Loudoun has lower rates of long commutes (24%).

```{r}
#| label: fig-traveltime
#| fig-cap: "More than a third of Fauquier commuters travel 45 minutes or more"
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart of the share of workers commuting 45 minutes or more. Bealeton is highest at 39%, followed by Culpeper and Fauquier at 37%, Prince William at 36%, Warrenton at 31%, Loudoun at 24%, and Virginia lowest at 18%. Fauquier is shown in blue and the two towns in coral."

tt <- wf$b08303 |>
  mutate(tot = estimate[variable == "B08303_001"], .by = GEOID) |>
  filter(variable %in% c("B08303_011", "B08303_012", "B08303_013")) |>
  summarize(n45 = sum(estimate), moe = sqrt(sum(moe^2)), tot = first(tot), .by = c(GEOID, NAME, geo_type)) |>
  mutate(share = n45 / tot,
         cv = (moe / 1.645) / n45 * 100) |>
  flag_reliability() |>
  mutate(place = case_when(GEOID == fauquier ~ "Fauquier", GEOID == "51047" ~ "Culpeper",
                           GEOID == "51153" ~ "Prince William", GEOID == "51107" ~ "Loudoun",
                           GEOID == "5183136" ~ "Warrenton", GEOID == "5105336" ~ "Bealeton",
                           GEOID == virginia ~ "Virginia"),
         grp = case_when(GEOID == fauquier ~ "Fauquier",
                         GEOID %in% unname(towns) ~ "Town", .default = "Other"),
         place = fct_reorder(place, share))

ggplot(tt, aes(share, place, fill = grp)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label_percent(accuracy = 1)(share)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3, color = "grey25") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1), expand = expansion(c(0, 0.12))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Fauquier = blue, Town = coral, Other = "grey75"), guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "More than a third of Fauquier commuters travel 45 minutes or more",
    subtitle = "Share of workers commuting 45+ minutes, 2024: <span style='color:#445ca9'>**Fauquier**</span> and <span style='color:#e76f52'>**study towns**</span>",
    caption = acs_cap("B08303"), x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda(flip_gridlines = TRUE)
```

Within the county, Bealeton commuters travel the farthest, with 39% of commuters traveling 45 minutes or more. Only 31% of Warrenton residents travel that long for work, reflecting Warrenton's greater share of local, in-town jobs, as well as proximity to transportation.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Town contrast: Warrenton and Bealeton
**Warrenton and Bealeton are demographically opposite** — Warrenton is older, and has more single-person and renter households, paired with lower incomes. Bealeton is younger and family-heavy with higher income (@fig-households, @fig-income-dist). **Affordability pressure** and the **demographic story** both play out differently in the two places.
:::
